chunks: And as for what was narrated - by Sa'd ibn Abdullah from al-Hasan ibn Ali from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from some of our companions from al-Rida (peace be upon him) who said:
I asked him about the person in ihram who has a companion who falls ill and shades his head; is it permissible for him to seek shade? He said, 'Yes.'

Thus it does not contradict the first report, because his saying 'is it permissible for him to seek shade' does not imply that only the ill person may seek shade; it is possible he meant: regarding this one who fell ill and shaded himself, was it permissible for him to do so or not? He said 'Yes'. And permission has been granted for women to shade themselves, as narrated.

key_terms.التَّظْلِيلُ: The act of shading (specifically allowed for women in ihram)
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمِ: The person in the state of ihram (ritual consecration for Hajj or Umrah)
key_terms.فَاعْتَلَّ: He fell ill or became weak

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a pilgrim in ihram to shade their head if they are ill?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Rida (AS), the issue of shading the head during ihram is clarified through a specific case of illness, demonstrating that the permission is not exclusive to the sick but applies generally unless restricted by other evidence. Shaykh al-Tusi uses this to resolve apparent contradictions in hadith literature by distinguishing between the specific context of the question and the general ruling. This highlights the Shia method of reconciling narrations by considering the implicit scope of the Imam's response.
